processing: Steamed green tea; some island producers stress light steaming (asamushi) to keep aroma, and shaded kabuse lots also exist.
harvest_season: Very early: first flush picking is reported from around March, which is why the island is known for hashiri shincha, the first new tea of the year.
appearance_dry: As is usual for sencha, fine dark green needles, varying by producer.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow-green, typical of lightly steamed tea.
appearance_wet: Soft, bright green leaf pieces, like other light-steamed sencha.
taste_profile: Shoju, the island's best-known cultivar, is described as having a milky, almost vanilla note and an unusual sweetness; blends are sold as gentle and rounded.

brewing.notes: Keep the water cool for early-season tea, whose delicate aroma is the whole point.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year, and timing is the selling point: hashiri shincha reaches the market from around March, ahead of most of the mainland. Buy it in the season it was picked; freshness is what you are paying for. The 'earliest in Japan' line comes from local promoters.
description:
Tanegashima-cha is green tea from Tanegashima, the island south of the Kagoshima mainland. Its warm climate gives it its identity: picking begins weeks before most of Japan, and the island promotes itself as the home of the country's earliest new tea.

The other reason to care is cultivars. Producers grow Shoju and Kuriwatase, rare names that local growers say are hardly found elsewhere. Shoju is the one to seek out, for its milky, vanilla-like sweetness.

Most of it is handled like sencha, and some makers stress a light steam for clean aroma. Brew it cool and short at first. It is a tea for fragrance and softness, so overheating it wastes what is special.

On the shelf you will see single-cultivar lots and house blends, often labelled たねがしま茶. Look for the cultivar and picking date, and take 'earliest' as a marketing word unless the date backs it up.
history:
Records of the island's tea industry are fairly thin in general references. The Shojuen farm presents itself as a tea garden with about a century of tradition.

Today's reputation rests on early-season shincha and on the island's unusual cultivars, with several small producers working on the island.
